Non-disclosure agreements - These are usually between two private parties, and in my experience it is often one person and one company. If someone violates a non-disclosure agreement, they could not be arrested but they could be sued by the aggrieved party in a civil court. I could see that if a person saw that a company was doing something illegal and reported it to the authorities, this right/obligation would supersede the non-disclosure agreement in civil court. I don't think this is the case if the aggrieved party is the US government. If the FBI hires you as a contractor to clean the carpets in one of their offices, I'm pretty sure you would be asked to sign a non-disclosure agreement and would not be able to take copious notes on what you saw there and just disclose it to the internet. I think you might be taking an idealized view of representatives. In the US the president is an absurdly powerful role. Here's a few things unique to that position:

  • Free publicity. The presidential role comes with an enormous amount of publicity. Anything the president wants to draw major attention to, he can. This attention in turn gets people interested and drives congress to act in a certain way. For instance if Ron Paul had become president he would have been able to enact changes towards the federal reserve not through unilateral action, but by being able to put the entire nation's eyes on the topic.

  • The veto. Everybody has their own legislative agenda. In a congress that's not going to unite enough for a veto-overturning supermajority on anything aside from corporate handouts, the veto becomes incredibly powerful as it means you anything the president doesn't want passed isn't going to get passed. This gives him effectively infinite room to gain 'favors.'

  • Executive orders. Executive orders, which incidentally are not specifically codified into our constitution or law anywhere but exist nonetheless, allow presidents enormous power. For instance FDR's gold act which obligated citizens to turn over all gold to the government was initially enacted through an executive order. That's huge. Following FDR these orders dropped off but have taken a sharp rise since George W and Obama have begun using them to pass and enforce their will in a semi arbitrary fashion. There seems to have been no desire from either side to clamp down on these, so we can expect they'll only grow in magnitude in the years and presidents to come.
